stem: What job does the underlined sentence do in this passage?
stimulus: For decades, immunologists assumed that the immune system's long-term memory belonged only to T cells and B cells, the cells that learn to recognize specific germs. Recent work has challenged that view. <u>In mice given a weakened tuberculosis vaccine, front-line immune cells called macrophages fought off an unrelated fungal infection more strongly months later.</u> This suggests that even the body's first responders can carry a kind of memory.
choices: It presents a finding that supports the challenge to the older view.
It states the older view that the rest of the passage goes on to question.
It describes the method researchers used to give the mice a vaccine.
It proves that macrophages remember every infection they have encountered.
explanation: Cover the underlined sentence and look at what's missing. The passage says an old view 'has been challenged' and then concludes that first responders 'can carry a kind of memory', but without the underlined sentence there is nothing to back that up. The sentence reports what happened to the mice, so it is a result, and that result is the evidence against the old view. Naming the role (a finding, not background or a method) is the first step in every 'function of the underlined sentence' question on the real test.

B.why: You picked the wrong sentence. The older view is in the first sentence, the one about T cells and B cells. The underlined sentence comes after 'Recent work has challenged that view' and works against that view rather than stating it.

C.why: This is the trap of matching words. 'Mice' and 'vaccine' appear in the sentence, but the sentence doesn't explain how anything was done. It reports what the macrophages did. That makes it a result, not a method.

D.why: The verb is too strong and the claim is too broad. The study tested one vaccine and one unrelated infection. That supports the idea that macrophages have 'a kind of memory', not that they remember every infection or that anything has been proved.

stem: What job does the underlined sentence do in this passage?
stimulus: On calm, clear nights, the ground loses heat quickly, and the air just above it cools faster than the air higher up. <u>Meteorologists call this layering, in which warmer air sits on top of cooler air, a temperature inversion.</u> Inversions can trap smoke and fog near the surface, which is why valleys often stay hazy until the morning sun warms the ground.
choices: It defines a term for the process the first sentence describes.
It explains why valleys stay hazy until the sun warms the ground.
It presents a result from a study of how smoke moves at night.
It disputes the first sentence's account of how the ground cools.
explanation: 'Meteorologists call this ... a temperature inversion' gives a name to something. 'This' points back to the cooling described in the first sentence. So the sentence defines a term, and the passage then uses that term in the last sentence. Spotting 'X is called Y' as a definition is the basic move behind the 'It defines a term' choices on the real test.

B.why: You read the wrong part of the text. The explanation about hazy valleys is in the last sentence. The underlined sentence only names the layering. It doesn't say what the layering causes.

C.why: This is the trap of matching words. The passage never mentions a study, and the underlined sentence reports no result. It gives a label to a process that was already described. 'Smoke' comes from a different sentence.

D.why: The relation is backward. The underlined sentence builds on the first sentence by naming what it described. Nothing in it argues against how the ground cools.

stem: What job does the underlined sentence do in this passage?
stimulus: Heavy stone grinding tools have been unearthed at a 9,000-year-old settlement in a river valley in southwest Asia. <u>It has been unclear whether the people who used them were grinding wild grasses or crops they had planted themselves.</u> To find out, a team examined starch grains trapped in the tools' worn surfaces and found that most came from wild barley rather than from domesticated barley.
choices: It raises the question that the study described next sets out to answer.
It reports the team's finding that the starch grains came from wild barley.
It gives background on where and when the grinding tools were found.
It argues that the people at the site never planted crops of any kind.
explanation: 'It has been unclear whether...' marks a gap in what researchers know. The next sentence begins 'To find out', which tells you the study is a response to that gap. So the underlined sentence poses the open question that the rest of the passage answers. Recognizing a sentence as the question rather than the answer is the core skill for 'open question' passages on the real test.

B.why: This is the trap of matching words. The finding about wild barley is in the last sentence. The underlined sentence asks the question that finding answers. Calling a question a result gives it the wrong role.

C.why: You picked the job of a different sentence. The first sentence gives the background about where and when the tools were found. The underlined sentence moves the passage forward by naming what isn't known yet.

D.why: The underlined sentence takes no side. It presents two possibilities. Even the later finding says only that 'most' grains were wild, so the passage never claims the people planted no crops at all.

stem: What job does the underlined sentence do in this passage?
stimulus: Engineers have traditionally focused on whether a bridge can carry heavy loads that stay still, such as the weight of its own deck and of stopped traffic. Yet forces that repeat in a steady rhythm can matter just as much. <u>When hundreds of runners crossed one newly built footbridge in step during a city race, its deck began to sway so much that officials closed it for repairs.</u> Designers now routinely test how structures respond to repeated pushes, not just to steady weight.
choices: It gives an example of the kind of force the previous sentence describes.
It describes the still loads that engineers have traditionally focused on.
It explains the method that designers now use to test new structures.
It shows that steady weight no longer matters in the design of bridges.
explanation: The sentence before it makes a general claim with no names or numbers: rhythmic, repeating forces matter. The underlined sentence is a specific case of that claim, since runners moving in step push on the bridge in a rhythm. A specific case placed after a general rule is an example. Telling an example apart from the claim it illustrates is what 'It illustrates' and 'It provides an example' choices test on the real exam.

B.why: You linked it to the wrong idea. Runners moving in step create a repeating force, the opposite of the 'loads that stay still' in the first sentence. The example supports the 'Yet' sentence, not the traditional focus.

C.why: This is the trap of matching words. Testing methods come up only in the last sentence. The underlined sentence tells what happened to one bridge, so it is an example, not a method.

D.why: This goes beyond the text. The passage says rhythmic forces matter 'just as much' and that designers test for them 'not just' steady weight, so steady weight still counts.
